column2: But Odysseus of many wiles stripped himself of his rags,
and leapt onto the great threshold, holding the bow and the quiver
full of arrows, and poured the swift arrows
out before his feet, and spoke among the suitors:
He spoke, and aimed a bitter arrow at Antinous.
He was just about to lift a fair cup,
a golden two-handled one, and already was handling it in his hands,
to drink the wine; and slaughter was not in his mind;
who would think that among men feasting,
one man among many, even if he were very strong,
would bring on him evil death and black fate?
Him Odysseus hit with an arrow, aiming at the throat,
and straight through the tender neck went the point.
He sank to one side, and the cup fell from his hand
as he was struck, and at once a thick jet of human blood
came through his nostrils; and quickly he from him the table
thrust away, striking it with his foot, and the food was spilled on the ground;
bread and roast meat were fouled. And the suitors
roared through the house when they saw the man fallen,
and sprang up from their chairs, stirred through the house,
looking everywhere at the well-built walls;
and nowhere was there a shield or stout spear to take.
And they railed at Odysseus with angry words:

Stranger, you shoot at men to your hurt; you will no longer meet
28	other contests; now for you sheer destruction is sure.
29	For you have now killed a man who was by far the best
30	of the youths in Ithaca; therefore here vultures will eat you.
So each man said, for they thought he had not meant
to kill the man; but the fools did not perceive
that the cords of destruction were fastened on them all.
Looking darkly at them spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

You dogs, you did not think I would come back home
36	from the land of the Trojans, because you wasted my house,
37	and lay with the maidservant women by force,
38	and, while I was still alive, wooed my wife,
39	neither fearing the gods who hold the broad heaven,
40	nor that any indignation of men would come hereafter;
41	now on all of you the cords of destruction are fastened.
So he spoke, and pale fear seized them all;
and each looked about for where he might escape sheer destruction.
And Eurymachus alone answered him and said:

If you are indeed Odysseus of Ithaca, come back,
46	you have spoken rightly of what the Achaeans did,
47	many wanton deeds in the halls, many in the field.
48	But he already lies dead who was the cause of all,
49	Antinous; for he urged on these deeds,
50	not so much in need of marriage nor desiring it,
51	but with other thoughts, which the son of Kronos did not fulfil for him,
52	that he might be king in the district of well-settled Ithaca
53	himself, and might kill your son by ambush.
54	But now he has been slain in due measure, and you spare your people;
55	and we will afterward make amends through the district,
56	for all that has been drunk and eaten in your halls,
57	each bringing a compensation of twenty oxen,
58	and bronze and gold we shall pay back, until your heart
59	is soothed; before that it is not blameworthy that you are angry.
Looking darkly at him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Eurymachus, not even if you gave me all your father's goods,
62	all that you now have and if you added others from somewhere,
63	not even so would I yet hold my hands from slaughter
64	before the suitors had paid for all their transgression.
65	Now there lies before you to fight
66	or flee, whoever may escape death and the fates;
67	but I think that none will escape sheer destruction.
So he spoke, and on the spot their knees and dear heart were loosened.
And Eurymachus spoke to them a second time:

Friends, this man will not hold back his unconquerable hands,
71	but since he has taken the well-polished bow and quiver,
72	he will shoot from the polished threshold, until he kills
73	us all; but let us think of battle.
74	Draw your swords and hold up the tables
75	against the swift-fated arrows; and let us all rush on him
76	together, to see if we can thrust him from the threshold and the doors,
77	and go through the town, and a shout would quickly arise;
78	then this man would soon shoot for the last time.
So speaking he drew his sharp sword
of bronze, sharpened on both sides, and leapt at him
crying terribly; but at the same moment godly Odysseus
shot an arrow, and hit him in the chest beside the nipple,
and fixed the swift shaft in his liver; and from his hand
the sword he dropped to the ground, and bent over the table
he fell doubled up, and spilled the food on the ground
and the two-handled cup; and he struck the earth with his forehead
in anguish of spirit, and with both feet
kicking he shook the chair; and a mist was poured over his eyes.
And Amphinomus rushed at glorious Odysseus,
springing straight against him, and drew his sharp sword,
to see if he could make him give way from the doors. But Telemachus
was ahead of him, striking him from behind with the bronze-tipped spear
between the shoulders, and drove it through his chest;
and he fell with a thud, and struck the ground with his whole forehead.
And Telemachus sprang away, leaving the long-shadowed spear
there in Amphinomus; for he feared lest one of the Achaeans,
as he drew out the long-shadowed spear, might rush at him
with a sword and stab him, or strike him bending forward.
He went running, and very quickly reached his dear father,
and standing near addressed him with winged words:

O father, now I shall bring you a shield and two spears
102	and an all-bronze helmet, fitted to the temples,
103	and I myself shall arm, going, and shall give to the swineherd
104	and to the cowherd others; for it is better to be armed.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Run and bring them, while I have arrows to defend myself,
107	lest they move me from the doors, alone as I am.
So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,
and went to the chamber, where his famous arms lay.
From there he took out four shields, and eight spears,
and four bronze helmets, thick with horsehair;
and he went carrying them, and very quickly reached his dear father.
And he himself first put the bronze about his body,
and in the same way the two servants put on the fair armour,
and stood beside wise Odysseus of many devices.
But he, so long as he had arrows to defend himself,
so long kept shooting one of the suitors in his house
at a time, aiming; and they fell thick one by one.
But when the arrows failed the archer lord,
he leaned the bow against the wall of the well-built hall
to stand against the shining gateway,
and himself put the four-layered shield about his shoulders,
and on his mighty head set the well-made helmet,
horse-tailed, and the crest nodded terribly above;
and took two stout spears tipped with bronze.
Now there was a side-door in the well-built wall,
and at the topmost threshold of the well-founded hall
there was a way into a passage, and well-fitted planks closed it.
This Odysseus bade the godly swineherd watch,
standing near it; for there was only one approach.
And Agelaus spoke among them, declaring to all:
Then Melanthius, the goatherd of goats, spoke to him in turn:

It is in no way possible, Agelaus nurtured by Zeus; for terribly near
137	are the fair doors of the courtyard and the difficult mouth of the passage;
138	and one man could hold back all, if he were stout.
139	But come, I shall bring you armour to put on
140	from the chamber; for inside, I think, and nowhere else
141	Odysseus and his shining son have laid the armour.
So saying Melanthius, the goatherd of goats, went up
to the storerooms of Odysseus by the clefts of the hall.
From there he took out twelve shields, and as many spears
and as many bronze helmets thick with horsehair;
and went, and very quickly carrying them gave them to the suitors.
And then the knees and dear heart of Odysseus were loosened,
when he saw them putting on armour and in their hands
brandishing long spears; and the task appeared great to him.
And at once he addressed Telemachus with winged words:

Telemachus, surely one of the women in the halls
152	is stirring up evil war against us two, or Melantheus.
Then prudent Telemachus answered him:

O father, I myself erred in this—and no one else
155	is to blame—who left the close-fitted door of the chamber
156	ajar; and their watcher was better than ours.
157	But go, godly Eumaeus, shut the door of the chamber
158	and see whether it is one of the women who does this,
159	or the son of Dolius, Melantheus, as I think.
So they spoke such things to one another,
and Melanthius, the goatherd of goats, went again to the chamber
to bring fair armour. And the godly swineherd noticed,
and at once spoke to Odysseus, who was near:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
165	that wretched man, whom we ourselves suspected,
166	is going to the chamber; tell me truly,
167	whether I shall kill him, if I prove the stronger,
168	or bring him here to you, that he may pay for the many
169	transgressions which he has devised in your house.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

I and Telemachus will hold the noble suitors
172	inside the halls, however eager they are.
173	You two, twisting back his feet and hands above,
174	cast him into the chamber, and fasten planks behind,
175	and tying a plaited rope to him
176	haul him up a high pillar and bring him near the beams,
177	that he may live long and suffer grievous pains.
So he spoke, and they heard him well and obeyed,
and went to the chamber, and he did not notice them inside.
He was searching for armour in the depth of the chamber,
and the two stood waiting on either side by the door-posts.
When Melanthius, the goatherd of goats, was stepping over the threshold,
with one hand carrying a fair helmet,
and with the other a broad old shield, spotted with mould,
of the hero Laertes, which he carried when young;
by then it was lying there, and the seams of the straps were loosened;
the two leapt on him and seized him and dragged him in
by the hair, and threw him on the floor, grieved at heart,
and bound his feet and hands with a heart-grieving bond
tightly twisting them back, right through, as bade
the son of Laertes, the much-enduring godly Odysseus;
and tying a plaited rope to him
they hauled him up a high pillar and brought him near the beams.
And mocking him you spoke, swineherd Eumaeus:

Now indeed, Melanthius, you will keep watch all night long,
196	lying on a soft bed, as befits you;
197	and early-born golden-throned Dawn will not escape you
198	rising from the streams of Oceanus, when you drive
199	goats for the suitors to prepare a feast in the house.
So he was left there, stretched in the deadly bond;
and the two, putting on their armour, closing the shining door,
went to wise Odysseus of many devices.
There, breathing fury, they stood, four on the threshold,
and inside the house many and valiant.
And to them near came Athena, daughter of Zeus,
likened to Mentor both in form and voice.
Odysseus rejoiced to see her and spoke a word:

Mentor, ward off ruin, and remember your dear comrade,
209	who did you good; and you are of my age.
So he spoke, thinking it was Athena, rouser of the host.
And the suitors from the other side shouted in the halls;
first Agelaus, son of Damastor, rebuked her:

Mentor, let not Odysseus persuade you with words
214	to fight the suitors and defend himself.
215	For thus I think our purpose will be fulfilled:
216	when we have killed these, father and son,
217	you will be killed among them, for what you intend
218	to do in the halls; you will pay with your own head.
219	And when with bronze we have taken away your strength,
220	all the possessions you have, inside and outside,
221	we shall mix with those of Odysseus; and your sons
222	we shall not allow to live in your halls, nor your daughters,
223	nor your faithful wife to walk about the town of Ithaca.
So he spoke, and Athena was angered still more at heart,
and rebuked Odysseus with angry words:

No longer, Odysseus, is your strength steady, nor any valour
227	such as when for white-armed, high-born Helen
228	nine years you fought the Trojans unceasingly always,
229	and killed many men in dread battle,
230	and by your counsel was taken Priam's wide-wayed city.
231	How now, when you have come to your house and possessions,
232	do you lament to be brave against the suitors?
233	But come here, friend, stand by me and see the deed,
234	that you may know what sort Mentor, son of Alcimus,
235	is among hostile men for repaying kindnesses.
She spoke, and did not yet give wholly the victory that turns,
but still tested the strength and valour
of both Odysseus and his glorious son.
And she herself, springing up, sat on the sooty rafter
of the hall, in the likeness of a swallow, facing them.
And the suitors were urged on by Agelaus, son of Damastor,
and Eurynomus and Amphimedon and Demoptolemus,
and Peisander son of Polyctor and wise Polybus;
for these were by far the best of the suitors in excellence,
of those who still lived and fought for their lives;
the others the bow and thick arrows had already subdued.
And Agelaus spoke among them, declaring to all:

Friends, soon this man will hold back his unconquerable hands;
249	and now Mentor has gone, having spoken empty boasts,
250	and they are left alone at the first doors.
251	So now do not all throw your long spears together,
252	but come, you six throw first, in case Zeus
253	may grant that Odysseus be hit and we win glory.
254	Of the others there is no care, when this man falls.
So he spoke, and they all threw as he bade,
eagerly; but Athena made them all in vain;
of them one hit the door-post of the well-built hall,
another the close-fitted door;
and another's bronze-weighted ash spear fell in the wall.
But when they had avoided the spears of the suitors,
among them began to speak the much-enduring godly Odysseus:

Friends, now I would say that we too
263	should throw at the crowd of suitors, who are eager
264	to slay us in addition to their former evils.
So he spoke, and they all threw their sharp spears,
aiming straight; Demoptolemus Odysseus,
and Euryades Telemachus, and Elatus the swineherd,
and Peisander the cowherd killed.
Then they all together bit the boundless ground,
and the suitors drew back to the inner part of the hall;
and the others rushed on, and drew their spears from the dead.
Again the suitors threw their sharp spears,
eagerly; but Athena made many of them in vain.
Of them one hit the door-post of the well-built hall,
another the close-fitted door;
and another's bronze-weighted ash spear fell in the wall.
And Amphimedon hit Telemachus on the hand at the wrist
grazing, and the bronze hurt only the surface of the skin.
And Ctesippus grazed Eumaeus' shoulder over the shield
with a long spear; and it flew over, and fell to the ground.
And they again around wise Odysseus of many devices
threw sharp spears into the crowd of suitors.
Then Odysseus, sacker of cities, hit Eurydamas,
and Telemachus Amphimedon, and the swineherd Polybus;
and then the cowherd hit Ctesippus
in the chest, and boasting spoke to him:

O son of Polytherses, lover of mockery, never again altogether
288	yielding to folly speak big, but leave
289	the word to the gods, since they are much stronger.
290	This is your guest-gift in exchange for the foot, which you once gave
291	to godlike Odysseus as he begged through the house.
So spoke the cowherd of the curved-horned cattle; and Odysseus
stabbed the son of Damastor at close quarters with his long spear.
And Telemachus stabbed Leocritus, son of Euenor,
with a spear in the middle of the flank, and drove the bronze through;
and he fell forward, and struck the ground with his whole forehead.
Then Athena held up the man-destroying aegis
on high from the roof; and their minds were frightened.
And they fled through the hall like herd cattle,
which the darting gadfly attacks and drives wild
in the season of spring, when the days are long.
But they, like vultures with curved talons and crooked beaks,
that come from the mountains and swoop on the birds;
these in the plain, cowering beneath the clouds, rush away,
and the vultures leap on them and destroy them, and there is no defence
nor flight; and men rejoice in the chase;
so they, rushing on the suitors through the house,
struck them down turning this way and that; and an ugly groan arose
from the heads being struck, and all the floor ran with blood.
And Leiodes, rushing up, took hold of Odysseus' knees,
and begging him addressed him with winged words:

I clasp your knees, Odysseus; do respect me and pity me;
313	for I say that never did I say or do anything wanton
314	to any of the women in the halls; but I tried to stop
315	other suitors, whoever did such things.
316	But they did not obey me to keep their hands from evil;
317	therefore by their wantonness they met a shameful fate.
318	But I, a soothsayer among them, having done nothing,
319	shall lie dead, so there is no gratitude afterward for good deeds.
Looking darkly at him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

If you boast to be a soothsayer among them,
322	you must often have prayed in the halls
323	that the end of my sweet homecoming be far from me,
324	and that my dear wife follow you and bear you children;
325	therefore you would not escape grievous death.
So speaking he took in his stout hand a sword
lying there, which Agelaus had dropped to the ground
when he was killed; with it he struck him in the middle of the neck.
And as he was still speaking, his head mingled with the dust.
And the son of Terpes, the singer, still sought to escape black fate,
Phemius, who sang among the suitors under compulsion.
He stood holding the clear-toned lyre in his hands
near the side-door; and he was torn in his mind,
whether to slip out of the hall to the altar
of Zeus of the courtyard, well made, where many
thigh-pieces of oxen Laertes and Odysseus had burned,
or to rush to Odysseus and beg at his knees.
And as he thought, this seemed to him the better course,
to clasp the knees of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
So he set the hollow lyre down on the ground
between the mixing-bowl and the silver-studded chair,
and himself rushing to Odysseus took hold of his knees,
and begging him addressed him with winged words:

I clasp your knees, Odysseus; do respect me and pity me;
345	you yourself will have grief hereafter, if you kill
346	a singer, who sing for gods and men.
347	I am self-taught, and a god planted in my mind songs
348	of every kind; and I am fit to sing to you
349	as to a god; therefore do not be eager to cut my throat.
350	And Telemachus too, your dear son, would say this,
351	that not willingly nor in need did I come to your house
352	to sing to the suitors after their feasts,
353	but far more and stronger men led me by compulsion.
So he spoke, and the sacred might of Telemachus heard him,
and at once spoke to his father, who was near:

Hold, and do not strike this blameless man with bronze;
357	and the herald Medon we shall save, who always
358	in our house took care of me when I was a child,
359	unless Philoetius has killed him or the swineherd,
360	or he met you as you raged through the house.
So he spoke, and Medon, knowing wise things, heard him;
for he lay crouched under a chair, and wrapped about him
the newly flayed hide of an ox, escaping black fate.
At once he rose from the chair, and quickly threw off the hide,
and rushing to Telemachus took hold of his knees,
and begging him addressed him with winged words:

Dear friend, here I am; hold, and tell your father
368	not to hurt me with sharp bronze in his great strength,
369	angry at the suitors, who wasted his
370	possessions in the halls, and in their folly did not honour you at all.
Smiling at him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Take courage, since this man has rescued you and saved you,
373	that you may know in your heart, and tell another also,
374	that doing good is much better than doing evil.
375	But go out of the halls and sit outside
376	away from the slaughter in the courtyard, you and the much-singing singer,
377	until I do in the house what I must.
So he spoke, and the two went out of the hall,
and sat down by the altar of great Zeus,
looking about everywhere, always expecting slaughter.
And Odysseus looked through his house, whether any man still
was hiding alive, escaping black fate.
But he saw them all in blood and dust,
many fallen, like fish, which fishermen
have drawn out of the grey sea onto a hollow beach
in a net of many meshes; and all of them
longing for the waves of the salt sea lie heaped on the sand;
and from them the shining sun takes away life;
so then the suitors lay heaped on one another.
Then Odysseus of many wiles spoke to Telemachus:

Telemachus, come, call me the nurse Eurycleia,
392	that I may say a word which is in my mind.
So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,
and shaking the door spoke to the nurse Eurycleia:
So he spoke, and her word was wingless,
and she opened the doors of the well-inhabited halls,
and went; and Telemachus led the way before.
Then she found Odysseus among the slain corpses,
stained with blood and gore like a lion,
which has been eating an ox of the field and comes away;
all his chest and cheeks on both sides
are bloody, and he is dreadful to look in the face;
so Odysseus was stained as to his feet and hands above.
And she, when she saw the corpses and the boundless blood,
made to cry out in triumph, since she saw a great deed;
but Odysseus restrained her and held her back, eager though she was,
and speaking to her addressed her with winged words:
Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:

Therefore I will tell you the truth, child.
421	fifty women there are in the halls,
422	maidservants, whom we have taught to do their work,
423	to card wool and to bear servitude;
424	of these twelve in all have gone to shamelessness,
425	honouring neither me nor Penelope herself.
426	Telemachus has only lately grown up, and his mother
427	did not allow him to give orders to the women servants.
428	But come, let me go up to the shining upper chamber
429	and tell your wife, on whom some god has cast sleep.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Do not wake her yet; but tell the women here
432	to come, those who before devised shameful things.
So he spoke, and the old woman went through the hall
to tell the women and urge them to come.
But he, calling Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
to himself, addressed them with winged words:

Begin now to carry out the corpses and bid the women help;
438	and then the very beautiful chairs and the tables
439	clean with water and porous sponges.
440	And when you have set all the house in order,
441	lead the maidservants out of the well-built hall,
442	between the round house and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
443	and strike them with long-edged swords, until you have taken
444	the life from all, and they forget Aphrodite,
445	whom they had under the suitors and lay with in secret.
So he spoke, and the women came all together,
bitterly lamenting, shedding abundant tears.
First they carried out the dead corpses,
and laid them under the portico of the well-fenced courtyard,
leaning them on one another; and Odysseus gave directions
himself, urging them on; and they carried them out, under compulsion.
And then the very beautiful chairs and the tables
they cleaned with water and porous sponges.
And Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
with hoes scraped the floor of the well-built house;
and the maidservants carried out the scrapings and put them outside.
And when they had put all the hall in order,
they led the maidservants out of the well-built hall,
between the round house and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
and drove them into a narrow space, whence there was no escape.
And prudent Telemachus began to speak among them:

May I not take the life from these women by a clean death,
463	who poured reproaches on my head
464	and on our mother, and lay with the suitors.
So he spoke, and the cable of a dark-prowed ship
he fastened to a great pillar and threw it round the round house,
stretching it high up, so that no one might touch the ground with her feet.
And as when long-winged thrushes or doves
fall into a snare set in a thicket,
as they seek their roost, and a hateful bed receives them,
so they held their heads in a row, and round all their
necks were nooses, that they might die most piteously.
They kicked with their feet for a little, not at all long.
And Melanthius they led out through the porch and the courtyard;
from him his nose and ears with pitiless bronze
they cut, and drew out his privy parts, for dogs to eat raw,
and cut off his hands and feet with angry heart.
Then they, having washed their hands and feet,
went to the house of Odysseus, and the deed was done;
and he spoke to his dear nurse Eurycleia:

Bring sulphur, old woman, cure of evils, bring me fire,
482	that I may purify the hall; and bid Penelope
483	come here with her women attendants;
484	and urge all the maidservants in the house to come.
Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:

Yes indeed, my child, this you have said in due measure.
487	But come, let me bring you a cloak and tunic, clothes,
488	and do not stand thus in the halls, with your broad shoulders
489	covered with rags; it would be blameworthy.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:
Fire first of all let there be for me in the halls.
So he spoke, and his dear nurse Eurycleia did not disobey,
and brought fire and sulphur; and Odysseus
thoroughly purified the hall and house and courtyard.
And the old woman went away through the fair house of Odysseus
to tell the women and urge them to come;
and they came from the hall holding torches in their hands.
They poured about him and welcomed Odysseus,
and kissed him lovingly on the head and shoulders
and grasped his hands; and sweet longing took him
for weeping and groaning, and he knew them all in his mind.
